title: Graceful degradation: quant soft-fallback probe
body:
Purpose:
This is a working note for the 'soft-fallback' experiments: try to avoid hard, binary fallback to FP16 when a low-precision kernel exhibits quality or stability regressions. Instead we want the runtime to degrade along a continuum (precision profile / kernel choice / batching adjustments) so client-visible quality and P99 latency change smoothly.

Context and motivation:
- We see user-facing 5–20% quality regressions in rare paths when AWQ/GPTQ INT8 kernels hit corner cases (long prompt + attention sparsity).
- Current strategy: immediate fallback to FP16 equivalent on error or on a heuristic threshold -> causes big latency spike and cost jump.
- Hypothesis: a staged fallback (soft-fallback) that attempts: (1) different kernel (safer but slightly slower), (2) narrower quant profile (higher precision for critical layers), (3) dynamic batch-size reduction, will reduce the magnitude of quality or latency shock while containing cost/regret.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Models: Llama-2-13b, Mistral-7b, Custom-chat-16b-proxy (internal test artifact).
- Quant profiles: AWQ-int8 (aggressive), GPTQ-int8 (balanced), FP8-mixed, FP16 baseline.
- Kernels: fast-kernel-v3 (high throughput), safe-kernel-1 (more conservative numeric path), vector-tiling (memory-friendly).
- Fallback stages tested (ordered):
  0) No fallback (baseline, allow failures)
  1) Kernel switch only (fast -> safe)
  2) Kernel + per-layer higher-precision for top-k layers (e.g., keep first/last 2 layers at FP16)
  3) As (2) + reduce batch size by 50% for affected request
  4) Full fallback to FP16 (current heavy-handed approach)

Metrics captured (per workload / seed prompts):
- Latency: P50 / P95 / P99 (ms)
- Throughput: tokens/sec under steady-state
- Cost proxy: GPU cycles consumed / effective token cost
- Quality: normalized cross-entropy vs FP16 (NCE), and application metric (chat-turn appropriateness score, human eval proxy), and short-term ROUGE/EM where applicable
- Failure modes: numeric exceptions, hallucination tokens count (heuristic), degenerate repetition score

Test harness notes:
- Small client-sim harness with 40 concurrent clients, Poisson arrivals, prompt length distribution drawn from production traces (median prompt 80 tokens, tail to 300).
- Synthetic edge cases: long context with repeated rare tokens to trigger KV-cache and attention sparsity issues.
- Each run: 60 minutes steady-state, repeated 5 seeds, collect per-request logs + microprofiles (kernel occupancy, CUDA memcopy times).

Representative results (summary numbers are median over seeds; numbers are illustrative but drawn from lab runs):
- Baseline (AWQ-int8 + fast-kernel-v3, no fallback):
  P50 14 ms, P95 92 ms, P99 320 ms, tokens/sec 420k, NCE delta vs FP16: +0.09 (worse), hallucination increase: +12%
  Failure rate (numeric exceptions): 0.7% of requests (mostly long-context).
- Hard fallback (immediate FP16):
  P50 28 ms, P95 160 ms, P99 640 ms, tokens/sec 210k, NCE delta 0.00 (by definition), cost proxy doubled, UX jitter: high
- Soft-fallback (stage 1: kernel switch only):
  P50 16 ms, P95 110 ms, P99 380 ms, tokens/sec 360k, NCE delta +0.03, failures dropped to 0.2%
- Soft-fallback (stage 2: kernel + per-layer brighten):
  P50 18 ms, P95 125 ms, P99 420 ms, tokens/sec 330k, NCE delta +0.01, hallucination +3%, failures ~0.05%
- Soft-fallback (stage 3: +batch reduce):
  P50 22 ms, P95 140 ms, P99 480 ms, tokens/sec 260k, NCE delta +0.005, failures ~0.01%

Interpretation: gradient of tradeoffs
- Kernel switch (cheap) removes most numeric failure cases with small latency cost and retains most throughput — good first line.
- Per-layer uplift gives better quality at moderate cost; tuning which layers to uplift matters and depends on model arch (e.g., Mistral benefits most from last-2-layer uplift).
- Batch reduction is expensive but helps p99 stability in long-burst contexts; best reserved as last soft-step before full FP16 fallback.

Microprofile observations:
- Fast-kernel-v3 shows 30–40% lower kernel execution time but 3x higher memory-copy stall on long contexts; safe-kernel-1 trades some arithmetic speed for fewer divergent branches and smaller activation oscillations.
- Switching kernels mid-request is not trivial: state layout (KV cache) needs translation for some kernel combinations — we instrumented a 6 ms translation overhead in the worst case. This influences whether kernel switch is net positive for short requests.

Notable edge findings:
- Some AWQ patterns produce very low-entropy attention matrices that cause integer overflow at accumulation step on older kernels — these are deterministic once prompted with a specific token pattern. Identifying those token fingerprints allows preemptive profile-based routing.
- FP8 mixed profiles occasionally cause subtle drift that appears after ~300 tokens — this suggests a small-amplitude bias accumulating; staged uplift of certain attention layers prevents drift in most runs.

Actionable playbook draft (runtime behavior recommendation):
1) Default: try aggressive AWQ-int8 + fast-kernel for short/typical requests (len < 150).
2) For requests that exceed len threshold OR hit attention-sparsity pattern score > 0.8 (new feature): attempt kernel switch to safe-kernel-1. If kernel switch succeeds and quality delta < 0.05 NCE, continue.
3) If score still bad after 1 retry: enable per-layer uplift (first/last 2 layers to FP16) and continue at reduced batch size if request latency budget is tight.
4) Only if all stages fail OR we observe numeric exception: full FP16 fallback. Log telemetry and surface to ops table for model-team review.

Suggested runtime knobs to add to control plane:
- per-model fallback policy (ordered list of stages + per-stage time budget)
- attention-sparsity scoring function (thresholds) and token fingerprint blacklist
- per-layer uplift config (which layers, and target precision)
- kernel-translation-cost estimator (to avoid switching on very short requests)

Open questions and next experiments:
- Can we precompute a tiny fast classifier on prompt tokens to predict likely numeric instability? Early experiments show 86% precision, 72% recall — needs more data.
- How does this pattern generalize across different generations of hardware (A100 vs H100)? Preliminary tests: H100 reduces translation overhead due to faster memcopy, making kernel switch more attractive.
- Can we compress per-layer uplift profiles into a compact taggable profile so model teams can ship suggested fallback plans with models?

Operational notes:
- Logging: need to start capturing per-request fallback path and stage durations (already added a feature flag in the runtime).
- Alerts: create a dashboard that tracks 'fallback escalation rate' for each model; arbitrarily set 0.5% as initial threshold for review.

Short TODOs:
- [ ] Add attention-sparsity score to production trace replayer (Diego)
- [ ] Run cross-hardware sweep (A100 vs H100) with stage 2 enabled (Priya)
- [ ] Prototype lightweight prompt fingerprint classifier, evaluate precision/recall (Elliot)
- [ ] Draft RFC for per-model fallback policy schema (Maya)

Notes to self: this doc is rough; will extract a clean RFC if the cross-hardware run confirms median numbers. Keep the harness configs and seeds checked into PR 742 for reproducibility.

Appendix: small ASCII table example (latency vs cost vs quality for quick glance)

Mode            | P99 (ms) | tokens/sec | NCE delta | cost proxy
---------------------------------------------------------------
AWQ+fast        | 320      | 420k       | +0.09     | 1.0
AWQ+fast->FP16  | 640      | 210k       | 0.00      | 2.0
AWQ+safe (switch)| 380     | 360k       | +0.03     | 1.2
AWQ+safe+uplift | 420      | 330k       | +0.01     | 1.4
AWQ+safe+uplift+batch | 480 | 260k       | +0.005    | 1.7

End of notes.
